claim: BMEL cells are bipotential precursors of the two epithelial hepatic lineages, derived from embryonic mouse liver.
source: BMEL, bipotential precursors of the two epithelial hepatic lineages, derived from embryonic mouse liver (Akkari et al., 2010; Strick-Marchand and Weiss, 2003; Strick-Marchand and Weiss, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Akkari et al., 2010; Strick-Marchand and Weiss, 2003; Strick-Marchand and Weiss, 2002).

claim: BMEL cells are not transformed and retain major characteristics of primary hepatic progenitors.
source: BMEL are not transformed and retain major characteristics of primary hepatic progenitors, including the capacity to repopulate a damaged adult liver (Strick-Marchand et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Strick-Marchand et al., 2004).

claim: Expression of oncogenic H-RasG12V is sufficient to transform a subset of BMEL clones.
source: We have previously reported that the expression of an oncogenic form of Ras (H-RasG12V) is sufficient to transform a subset of BMEL clones (Akkari et al., 2012; Bacevic et al., 2019), including the ones used for the current study.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Akkari et al., 2012; Bacevic et al., 2019).

claim: BMEL cells used in this study express p19ARF and wild-type p53, but not p16-INK4A.
source: These cells express p19ARF and wild-type p53, but not p16-INK4A (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), which could account for their escape from Ras-induced senescence (Xue et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and a citation to prior work (Xue et al., 2007).

claim: Cellular phenotypes are sensitive to Ras oncogene dosage.
source: Because cellular phenotypes are sensitive to the Ras oncogene dosage (Kerr et al., 2016; Mueller et al., 2018) and the signalling intensity of its downstream effector, the MAPK Erk pathway (Dikic et al., 1994; Traverse et al., 1994), we asked whether a specific level of RasG12V expression was required for hepatic tumour growth in vivo.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Kerr et al., 2016; Mueller et al., 2018).

claim: The fluorescence intensity of Venus and mCherry markers faithfully reflects Ras oncogene mRNA levels.
source: As expected, the expression levels of the fluorescent markers faithfully reflected the Ras oncogene mRNA levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 2)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mean levels of RasG12V protein were different in RasLOW versus RasHIGH populations.
source: the mean levels of RasG12V protein were different in the RasLOW versus the RasHIGH populations, as shown for RasLOW-Cherry and RasHIGH-Venus in Figure 1A.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Neither the level of Ras expression nor the nature of the co-expressed fluorescent protein altered the in vitro proliferation rate of transformed BMEL cells.
source: Importantly, neither the level of Ras expression nor the nature of the co-expressed fluorescent protein altered the in vitro proliferation rate of the transformed BMEL cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: RasHIGH cells gave significantly more colonies than RasLOW cells in soft agar assay.
source: Ras-transformed cells grew in soft agar, with the RasHIGH cells giving significantly more colonies than their RasLOW counterparts in this surrogate assay of transformation (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Oncogenic Ras had no effect on AKTS473 and GSKbS9 phosphorylation in BMEL cells.
source: Oncogenic Ras had no effect on AKTS473 and the GSKbS9, two downstream targets of PI(3)K that were strongly phosphorylated both in the parental and in the Ras-transformed cells.
evidence: The claim is based on phosphoprotein array data described in the text and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: No differences were detected for JNK and p38 pathway components between parental and Ras-transformed BMEL cells.
source: Similarly, no differences were detected for JNK and p38 pathway components.
evidence: The claim is based on phosphoprotein array data described in the text.

claim: Ras signalling gave rise to a strong increase in the phosphorylation of Rsk 1 and 2.
source: In contrast, although this assay did not reveal increased MEK or Erk activation, Ras signalling gave rise to a strong increase in the phosphorylation of Rsk 1 and 2, which are downstream targets of MAPK Erk signalling.
evidence: The claim is based on phosphoprotein array data described in the text and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Ras oncogene dosage translates into differences in Ras/MAPK Erk signalling as evidenced by distinct transcriptional signatures of Erk target genes.
source: Moreover, while the proteomic array assay was not sufficiently sensitive to distinguish between the RasLOW and RasHIGH signalling, the oncogenic dosage did translate into differences of the Ras/MAPK Erk signalling, as evidenced by distinct transcriptional signatures of known Erk delayed early target genes (Brant et al., 2017; Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D and a citation to prior work (Brant et al., 2017).

claim: RNAseq analysis identified over 1000 genes modulated by RasG12V signalling in hepatic progenitor cells.
source: Setting the thresholds at fold change log2=1.5 and p-value <0.01 identified over 1000 genes modulated by RasG12V signalling in these hepatic progenitor cells (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: 160 genes were modulated by Ras independently of its mean expression level.
source: The expression of 160 genes was modulated by Ras independently of its mean expression level in the tested population (Figure 1E left, Supplementary file 1a), thus representing a gene signature for the low threshold Ras/MAPK signalling.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 1E and Supplementary file 1a.

claim: 65 genes were modified only in RasHIGH cells, requiring high-intensity Ras signalling for mRNA accumulation.
source: In a second group of 65 genes, target gene expression was modified only in the RasHIGH cells (Figure 1E middle, Supplementary file 1b). For these genes, a high-intensity Ras signalling is required for the mRNA accumulation.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 1E and Supplementary file 1b.

claim: Six genes showed gradually increased expression in RasLOW and RasHIGH cell populations.
source: We identified six genes (Al467606, Aim2, Dynap, Htra3, Itgb7, Tspan13) whose expression was gradually increased in RasLOW and RasHIGH cell populations (Figure 1E right, Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 1E and Supplementary file 1c.

claim: Nine genes showed gradually repressed expression in RasLOW and RasHIGH cell populations.
source: Similarly, we found nine genes (Ppp2r2b, Cbr1, Pmp22, Ptp4a3, Pmaip1, Thbs1, Akap12, Sulf2, Crip2) the expression of which was gradually repressed.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data described in the text.

claim: Orthotopic injections of 10^5 BMEL-Ras cells into immunocompromised recipients systematically gave rise to hepatocellular tumours within 3-4 weeks.
source: Orthotopic injections of 105 BMEL-Ras cells into immunocompromised recipients systematically gave rise within 3–4 weeks to hepatocellular tumours at the site of injection as well as to frequent extrahepatic growth in the peritoneal cavity.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations described in the text.

claim: RasHIGH cells gave rise to significantly larger tumours than RasLOW cells.
source: In accordance with their superior capacity for anchorage-independent growth (Figure 1B), the RasHIGH cells gave rise to significantly larger tumours than their RasLOW counterparts, indicating that high level of Ras signalling conferred a selective advantage in vivo.
evidence: The claim is supported by tumour volume data described in the text and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The in vivo seeding efficiencies of RasHIGH and RasLOW cells were indistinguishable at 5 days post-injection.
source: The in vivo seeding efficiencies of RasHIGH and RasLOW cells were indistinguishable, since equal numbers of Venus and mCherry-labelled cells were detected at early times (5 days) post-injection (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: RasHIGH cells became the dominant population in tumours at day 10 and day 21 post-injection.
source: However, as the tumours grew, a clear imbalance between the two populations became apparent, with RasHIGH cells becoming the dominant population in tumours already at day 10, which was further confirmed in full-grown tumours 21 days post-injection (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Switching fluorescent labels between RasHIGH and RasLOW cells had no impact on the dominance of RasHIGH cells.
source: This was not due to an artefactual effect of the fluorescent markers, as switching the fluorescent labels between the RasHIGH and RasLOW cells had no impact on the dominance of RasHIGH cells.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations described in the text and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Both Venus+ and mCherry+ cellular populations composing the tumour expressed identical levels of RasG12V oncogene.
source: Interestingly, RTqPCR analysis specific for the RasG12V revealed that both cellular populations composing the tumour expressed identical level of the oncogene (Figure 2C right panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by RTqPCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Selective pressures during in vivo tumour growth allow expansion of a population with a defined level of Ras oncogene expression.
source: This suggests that selective pressures operating during the in vivo tumour growth allow the expansion of a population with a defined level of Ras oncogene expression, independently of which parental population they originate from.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that both populations express identical Ras levels in tumours.

claim: Cell lines established from orthotopic tumours maintained high levels of Ras expression in vitro.
source: Finally, cell lines established from the orthotopic tumours maintained the high level of Ras expression in vitro (Figure 2D), providing further support to the idea of pre-existing clones undergoing selection in vivo.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Extrahepatic tumours in the peritoneal cavity morphologically resemble paired liver tumours.
source: Indeed, in addition to intrahepatic tumour spread, we consistently observed tumours in the peritoneal cavity, morphologically resembling the paired liver tumours (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by images shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Peritoneal lavage performed after surgery contained low but detectable numbers (<0.5%) of Venus-labelled cells.
source: Extrahepatic tumours likely arose from cell leakage during the surgical procedure of intrahepatic injection, since peritoneal lavage performed after surgery contained low but detectable numbers (<0.5%) of Venus-labelled cells.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations described in the text.

claim: RasLOW cells gave significantly smaller hepatic tumours than RasHIGH cells, but this difference was abolished for peritoneal tumours.
source: Strikingly, whereas RasLOW cells gave significantly smaller hepatic tumours than RasHIGH cells, this difference was abolished with regard to peritoneal tumours (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by tumour volume data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Mean level of RasG12V expression was significantly higher in primary versus peritoneal tumours.
source: RTqPCR analyses confirmed the increased oncogenic dosage in the in vivo-grown cells compared to the in vitro-grown parental ones and revealed a significantly higher mean level of RasG12V expression in the primary versus the peritoneal tumours (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by RTqPCR data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Mean level of oncogene expression was independent of the origin of engrafted cells (RasHIGH versus RasLOW populations).
source: Strikingly, the mean level of the oncogene expression was again independent of the origin of the engrafted cells (i.e. RasHIGH versus RasLOW populations).
evidence: The claim is based on RTqPCR data described in the text and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Transcriptomic profiling identified approximately 160 genes differentially expressed in liver and peritoneal tumour cells.
source: This analysis identified approximately 160 genes differentially expressed in the liver and peritoneal tumour cells (log2 fold change >1; p<0.05; Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data described in the text and in Supplementary file 1d.

claim: GO analysis identified 27 enriched gene sets (25 in liver and 2 in peritoneum).
source: GO analysis using GSEA identified 27 enriched gene sets (25 in liver and 2 in peritoneum; p-value <0.01 and FDR <0.1. Supplementary file 1e).
evidence: The claim is supported by GSEA analysis described in the text and in Supplementary file 1e.

claim: MAPK signalling is increased in liver tumours compared to peritoneal tumours.
source: Importantly, it confirmed the increase of MAPK signalling in the liver and identified apoptotic processes and the regulation of the immune response among the gene sets differentially regulated in the two locations (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Both hepatic and peritoneal tumours were highly proliferative.
source: Both the hepatic and the peritoneal tumours were highly proliferative (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by Ki67 staining data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Hepatic tumours contain a higher proportion of cleaved caspase 3-positive cells than peritoneal tumours.
source: Interestingly, while the cultured BMEL cells expressing either high or low levels of the RasG12V oncogene have comparable, low, apoptotic indexes, hepatic tumours contain a higher proportion of cleaved caspase 3-positive cells than their peritoneal counterparts (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by caspase 3 staining data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Caspase 3-positive cells often surround large necrotic areas in liver tumours.
source: Moreover, in the liver, and much less so in the peritoneum, caspase 3-positive cells often surround large necrotic areas, indicating that the cell death in an expanding liver tumour is quite substantial, suggesting an evolutionary trade-off for the high oncogene dosage in the liver tumours.
evidence: The claim is based on histological observations described in the text and shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Cibersortx deconvolution did not show strong differences in numbers of intra-tumoural macrophages at liver and peritoneal locations.
source: Cibersortx deconvolution of the immune component of the stroma (Newman et al., 2019) did not show strong differences in the numbers of intra-tumoural macrophages at the two locations (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Cibersortx analysis shown in Figure 4A and a citation to the method (Newman et al., 2019).

claim: RTqPCR profiling of macrophage polarization markers suggested a more immunosuppressive, less inflammatory microenvironment in the peritoneum.
source: However, independent RTqPCR profiling of macrophage polarization markers did suggest a more immunosuppressive, less inflammatory microenvironment in the peritoneum (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by RTqPCR data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: A larger proportion of mature, activated dendritic cells were present in peritoneal tumours compared to liver tumours.
source: Indeed, our data suggested that a larger proportion of mature, activated dendritic cells (DCs), as compared to immature ones, were present in this organ (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Cibersortx analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Peritoneal DCs showed an increase in proliferation compared to liver DCs.
source: Flow cytometry analyses confirmed that while the total number of DCs (defined as CD45+ CD11b+ CD11c+ MHCIIhigh CD24+F4/80-) was not significantly different between the two TME, these cells showed an increase in proliferation in the peritoneum (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Peritoneal DCs contained lower levels of MFG-E8 compared to liver DCs.
source: Furthermore, the peritoneal DCs contained lower levels of the milk-fact globule-EGFVIII (MFG-E8), a factor known to limit DC immunogenic potential (Figure 4D; Baghdadi et al., 2012; Peng and Elkon, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4D and citations to prior work (Baghdadi et al., 2012; Peng and Elkon, 2012).

claim: Peripherally recruited monocyte-derived macrophages (F4/80low) were significantly enriched in liver tumours.
source: The content of peripherally recruited monocyte-derived macrophages presenting low expression of F4/80, defined as CD45+CD11b+Ly6G-Ly6C-F4/80low, was significantly enriched in liver tumours (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Differentiated, tissue resident-like F4/80high macrophages showed a tendency for enrichment in peritoneal HCC.
source: On the other hand, the differentiated, tissue resident-like, F4/80high macrophages showed a tendency for enrichment in the peritoneal HCC.
evidence: The claim is based on flow cytometry data described in the text.

claim: F4/80high peritoneal macrophages displayed superior proliferative capacity and activation phenotype compared to liver macrophages.
source: Interestingly, F4/80high peritoneal macrophages displayed a superior proliferative capacity (Ki67+) and activation phenotype (MHCII+, CD115+) compared to liver macrophages (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: No peritoneal tumour growth was detected in immunocompetent C57BL/6 mice, while 50% of nude mice developed macroscopic peritoneal tumours.
source: However, in contrast to nude mice, of which 50% developed macroscopic peritoneal tumours, no growth at a metastatic location was detected in immunocompetent recipients.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data described in the text and shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Four genes (Ceacam1, Csn3, Selp, Tmem252) were specifically induced by high-intensity Ras signalling both in RasHIGH cells and in liver tumours.
source: Out of four genes (Ceacam1, Csn3, Selp, Tmem252) that corresponded to this criterion, we focused our attention on CEACAM1 (carcinoembryonic antigen-related cell adhesion molecule 1), a gene widely expressed in many cancer types and whose expression level has been reported to correlate with tumour progression (Dankner et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptomic data described in the text and shown in Figure 5A, and a citation to prior work (Dankner et al., 2017).

claim: CEACAM1 is expressed on the surface of several immune cell subsets, including macrophages, T lymphocytes, and NK cells.
source: It is also expressed on the surface of several immune cell subsets, including macrophages, T lymphocytes, and NK cells, where homophilic interactions with the CEACAM1+ tumour cells abrogate NK-mediated cytotoxicity (Helfrich and Singer, 2019; Markel et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Helfrich and Singer, 2019; Markel et al., 2002).

claim: CEACAM1 expressing cells were highly enriched in CD45neg cells in liver tumours (30.1±2.4%) compared to peritoneal tumours (14.2±3%).
source: CEACAM1 expressing cells were highly enriched in this population in the liver as compared to peritoneal tumours, corresponding respectively to 30.1±2.4% (mean ± SEM) and 14.2±3% (mean ± SEM) of CD45neg cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Mean fluorescent intensities of CEACAM1 labelling in Venus+ populations were indistinguishable between liver and peritoneal tumours.
source: Strikingly, the mean fluorescent intensities of the CEACAM1 labelling in the Venus+ populations were indistinguishable between the tumours at the two locations.
evidence: The claim is based on flow cytometry data described in the text and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: NK cells infiltrate hepatic tumours but tend to remain in the periphery of peritoneal tumours.
source: Interestingly, while difference in the NK cell content in the primary and peritoneal tumours did not reach statistical significance in the deconvolution of stromal cells RNAseq (Figure 4A), immunofluorescence staining revealed distinct distribution of these cells: whereas NK infiltrate the hepatic tumours, they apparently tend to remain in the periphery of the peritoneal ones (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: RasHIGH cells were less sensitive to NK-mediated cell death than RasLOW cells in ex vivo cytotoxicity assays.
source: As predicted by our hypothesis, the RasHIGH cells were indeed less sensitive to NK-mediated cell death than their RasLOW counterparts.
evidence: The claim is supported by NK cytotoxicity assay data described in the text and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The majority of NSG mice displayed comparable tumour volumes at liver and peritoneal locations.
source: As in the nude mice, the NSG background was permissive for peritoneal metastatic-like growth, however, the majority of the animals displayed comparable tumour volumes at the two locations (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by tumour volume data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The number of caspase 3-positive cells was low for both liver and peritoneal tumours in NSG animals.
source: Consistently, the number of caspase 3-positive cells was low for both liver and peritoneal tumours in NSG animals (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Hepatic tumours in NSG background tolerated lower levels of CEACAM1 expression compared to nude mice.
source: In support of this contention, compared to the nude mice, the hepatic tumours in the NSG background tolerated lower levels of CEACAM1 expression, while there was no significant difference for the peritoneal tumours between the two genetic backgrounds.
evidence: The claim is supported by RTqPCR data described in the text and shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The difference between CEACAM1 expression in hepatic and peritoneal tumours was diminished but not abolished in NSG animals.
source: Of note, however, the difference between CEACAM1 expression in the hepatic and peritoneal tumours was diminished, but not abolished in the NSG animals (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by RTqPCR data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: CEACAM1-driven NK inhibition participates in clonal selection but is not the sole element of advantage afforded by high oncogene dosage.
source: Altogether, these results suggest that CEACAM1-driven NK inhibition participates in the clonal selection, but is not the sole element of the advantage afforded by the high oncogene dosage.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that differences in CEACAM1 expression persist in NSG mice.

claim: Variations in signal intensity, duration, and tissue-specific context give rise to distinct cellular outcomes in Ras/MAPK Erk signalling.
source: Moreover, variations in signal intensity, duration, and tissue-specific context give rise to distinct cellular outcomes (Lenormand et al., 1993; Marshall, 1995; Pouysségur et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Lenormand et al., 1993; Marshall, 1995; Pouysségur et al., 2002).

claim: Activating Ras mutations are rare in HCC (2-4% of patients).
source: Although mutations of Ras GTPases are found in only 2–4% of HCC patients, multiple activators and regulators of the pathway, such as FGF19, RSK2, RASAL1, RASSF1, and DUSPs, are more frequently mutated.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about HCC genetics described in the text.

claim: The Ras/MAPK pathway is estimated to be activated in 40% of HCC.
source: Altogether, the Ras/MAPK is estimated to be activated in 40% of HCC (Delire and Stärkel, 2015; Lim et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Delire and Stärkel, 2015; Lim et al., 2018).

claim: Activation of Ras/MAPK Erk signalling is an essential feature of proliferating cells.
source: Activation of Ras/MAPK Erk signalling is an essential feature of proliferating cells (Pagès et al., 1993) and the genetic abrogation of several of the components of the pathway gives rise to embryonic lethality due to a decrease in signal intensity (Dorard et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Pagès et al., 1993; Dorard et al., 2017).

claim: Strong Erk signal is protective in response to loss of anchorage, while moderate signal is required for anoikis.
source: This has been shown for example in response to the loss of anchorage, where strong Erk signal is protective, while a moderate one is required for anoïkis (Zugasti et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Zugasti et al., 2001).

claim: Excessive Erk activation can provoke cell cycle arrest or senescence.
source: However, excessive Erk activation can be detrimental to the cell, provoking cell cycle arrest or senescence (Serrano et al., 1997; Woods et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Serrano et al., 1997; Woods et al., 1997).

claim: Only 5% of Ras needs to be activated to give rise to full activation of Erk.
source: For example, although only 5% of the small GTPase Ras needs to be activated to give rise to full activation of Erk (Hallberg et al., 1994), a clear dosage effect has been reported in pancreatic and lung tumours for activating Ras mutations (East et al., 2021; Kerr et al., 2016; Mueller et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Hallberg et al., 1994; East et al., 2021; Kerr et al., 2016; Mueller et al., 2018).

claim: Amplifications of wild-type Ras allele result in allelic imbalance and modulation of oncogenic Ras mutant activity, leading to distinct cellular phenotypes.
source: Moreover, amplifications of the wild-type allele of Ras that give rise to an allelic imbalance and the consequent modulation of the activity of the oncogenic Ras mutants result in distinct cellular phenotypes (Ambrogio et al., 2018; Bremner and Balmain, 1990).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Ambrogio et al., 2018; Bremner and Balmain, 1990).

claim: Inactivating mutations of Rsk2 participate in shaping tumoural phenotype in HCC.
source: Of note, whereas activating Ras mutations are rare in HCC (Zucman-Rossi et al., 2015), alterations in the intensity of MAPK Erk signalling participate in shaping the tumoural phenotype, as revealed by inactivating mutations of Rsk2, which is both an ERK target and a negative regulator of the pathway (Chan et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Zucman-Rossi et al., 2015; Chan et al., 2021).

claim: HCC is classified among tumours with significant Ras pathway activation phenotype.
source: Moreover, a recent analysis of transcriptional signatures classified HCC among tumours with significant Ras pathway activation phenotype (East et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (East et al., 2021).

claim: Strong versus weak Ras-driven transcriptional signature has predictive value in HCC.
source: Because the same report highlighted the predictive value of strong versus weak Ras-driven transcriptional signature, it is relevant to model these phenotypes in HCC by controlled dosage of the Ras oncogene, as we have done in this study.
evidence: The claim is based on a citation to prior work (East et al., 2021) mentioned in the previous sentence.

claim: Resident NK cells acquire cytolytic functions mediated through TNFα and granzyme B during hepatotropic viral infections, cirrhotic pathology, and HCC.
source: Resident NK cells acquire cytolytic functions mediated through TNFα and granzyme B during hepatotropic viral infections, cirrhotic pathology, and HCC (Sällberg and Pasetto, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Sällberg and Pasetto, 2020).

claim: Viral adaptation to NK-mediated attack includes suppression of NK function through CEACAM1-mediated blockade.
source: The viral adaptation to the NK-mediated attack includes the suppression of their function through the CEACAM1-mediated blockade of their activity (Suda et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Suda et al., 2018).

claim: Peritoneal resident cells resemble immature splenic NK cells.
source: In contrast to the liver, the peritoneal resident cells resemble immature splenic NK cells (Gonzaga et al., 2011), which may account for a lesser involvement of these cells in anti-tumour immunity in this location, as suggested by our data.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Gonzaga et al., 2011).

claim: Only lung adenocarcinoma with strong Ras activating signature respond to inhibitors of the MAPK Erk pathway.
source: Similarly, only lung adenocarcinoma with a strong Ras activating signature respond to inhibitors of the MAPK Erk pathway (East et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (East et al., 2021).

claim: There are over 200 ongoing clinical trials on NK cell-based therapies for solid tumours, including HCC.
source: Moreover, there is a rising interest in the use of NK cell-based therapies, largely because of their considerably lower toxicity in comparison to T-cell transfer (reviewed in Xie et al., 2020), translating into over 200 ongoing clinical trials on solid tumours, including HCC (https://www.clinicaltrials.gov/).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a review (Xie et al., 2020) and reference to clinicaltrials.gov.

claim: BMEL cells were isolated from C57BL/6xC3H E14 embryonic mouse female liver.
source: BMEL cells were isolated from C57BL/6xC3H E14 embryonic mouse female liver, as described in Strick-Marchand and Weiss, 2002.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental method and is supported by a citation to prior work (Strick-Marchand and Weiss, 2002).

claim: Human H-RasG12V cDNA sequence was cloned into LeGO-iV2 and LeGO-iC2 bicistronic vectors.
source: Human H-RasG12V cDNA sequence was cloned into LeGO-iV2 and LeGO-iC2 bicistronic vectors (Addgene #27344 and #27345, respectively).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental method.

claim: Orthotopic injections of 5000 NRASG12D p53KO cells in C57BL/6J mice gave rise to comparable macroscopic liver tumours within 3 weeks as in nude mice.
source: Orthotopic allografts of 5000 cells performed in parallel on immunocompetent and immunodeficient mice gave rise to comparable macroscopic liver tumours within 3 weeks (Figure 4G).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Transcriptomic profiling of stromal cells revealed 2260 genes differentially expressed between liver and peritoneal tumours.
source: As expected, comparison of transcriptomic profiles from stromal cells of liver and peritoneal tumours pinpointed higher diversity (2260 genes for log2 fold change >1; p<0.05; Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The Ras/MAPK Erk pathway is activated in a large proportion of human tumours.
source: The MAPK Erk pathway, which is activated in a large proportion of human tumours, is a prototypic example of distinct cell fates being driven by signal intensity.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about cancer biology.

claim: Significantly higher Ras expression was observed in primary as compared to secondary, metastatic sites.
source: Indeed, significantly higher Ras expression was observed in primary as compared to secondary, metastatic sites, despite the apparent evolutionary trade-off of increased apoptotic death in the liver that correlated with high Ras dosage.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data described throughout the manuscript.

claim: Increased apoptotic death in the liver correlated with high Ras dosage.
source: Indeed, significantly higher Ras expression was observed in primary as compared to secondary, metastatic sites, despite the apparent evolutionary trade-off of increased apoptotic death in the liver that correlated with high Ras dosage.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Fast peritoneal tumour growth in the immunocompromised setting is abrogated in immunocompetent animals due to efficient antigen presentation by peritoneal dendritic cells.
source: Analysis of the immune tumour microenvironment at the two locations suggests that fast peritoneal tumour growth in the immunocompromised setting is abrogated in immunocompetent animals due to efficient antigen presentation by peritoneal dendritic cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that peritoneal tumours do not develop in immunocompetent mice and the finding of activated DCs in the peritoneum.

claim: Strong MAPK signalling is required in primary liver tumours to resist elimination by NK cells.
source: Furthermore, our data indicate that, in contrast to the metastatic-like outgrowth, strong MAPK signalling is required in the primary liver tumours to resist elimination by NK (natural killer) cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing RasHIGH cells are less sensitive to NK-mediated killing and are selected in liver tumours.

claim: Tumour subclonal heterogeneity is defined by cancer cells' intrinsic properties and phenotypic adaptations to extrinsic signals from the microenvironment.
source: Tumour subclonal heterogeneity is defined by cancer cells' intrinsic properties and by phenotypic adaptations to extrinsic signals from the microenvironment (Marusyk et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Marusyk et al., 2020).

claim: Specific environments are shaped by physiological constraints imposed by tumour localization and dynamic interactions with the growing tumour.
source: Specific environments are shaped by the physiological constraints imposed by the tumour localization and by the dynamic interactions with the growing tumour (Gerstung et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Gerstung et al., 2020).

claim: The environment impacts tumour phenotype by triggering adaptive responses from plastic cancer cells.
source: The environment impacts the tumour phenotype, first by triggering adaptive responses from the highly plastic cancer cells (Pastushenko and Blanpain, 2019) and second, by exerting selective pressures, leading to expansion of some, and elimination of other, tumoural subclones (Janiszewska et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Pastushenko and Blanpain, 2019; Janiszewska et al., 2019).

claim: Quantitative aspects leading to differences in oncogenic signal transduction intensity within clonal tumour cell populations are understudied.
source: While the notion of inter- and intra-tumour heterogeneities and their consequences for personalized medicine have gained a strong momentum in the last decade (Losic et al., 2020; Molina-Sánchez et al., 2020), quantitative aspects leading to differences in the intensity of oncogenic signal transduction within the selected, clonal tumour cell populations (see e.g. Gross et al., 2019) are so far understudied.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Losic et al., 2020; Molina-Sánchez et al., 2020; Gross et al., 2019).

claim: HCC has been classified into several classes defined by genomic and physiopathological characteristics.
source: For example, hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) has been classified into several classes, defined by their genomic and physiopathological characteristics (Llovet et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Llovet et al., 2021).

claim: Mutations that activate the β-catenin pathway or inactivate p53 tumour suppressor fall neatly into defined HCC categories.
source: While some oncogenic driver mutations fall neatly in such defined categories, for example, mutations that activate the β-catenin pathway or that inactivate the p53 tumour suppressor (Zucman-Rossi et al., 2015), others are frequently present in several different HCC types.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Zucman-Rossi et al., 2015).
